## Introduction

Every content-addressable system in computing today generates identifiers through a hash function. Storage engines use SHA-256 of content as the record key. Distributed systems use hash-based identifiers for node membership. Databases maintain hash indexes for fast lookup. The approach is universal, and it carries a universal cost: approximately 10,000 gate equivalents and 64-75 cycles for each identifier generation in hardware; 200-300 nanoseconds per operation in software.

This paper demonstrates that for the narrow task of identity generation -- creating a unique, deterministic identifier from structured data -- the hash function can be replaced by a closed-form coordinate composition that is 115x faster in software and approximately 30x cheaper in gates. The replacement is not cryptographic. Preimage resistance, authentication, encryption, and signature verification remain unchanged. Only identity generation is affected.

The Tagma coordinate space, defined in the whitepaper [@tagma-wp], provides a 16-bit deterministic mapping from three independent axes to a unique identifier with zero collisions by construction.

## The Problem: SHA-256 as Default Identity Generator

SHA-256 dominates identity generation not because it is optimal for the task, but because no practical alternative existed. The hash function performs two distinct roles:

1. **Deterministic mapping**: same input always produces same output
2. **Cryptographic security**: preimage resistance, collision resistance, avalanche effect

For identity generation, role 1 is essential and role 2 is incidental. A storage engine needs to know that two records with the same key are the same record. It does not need to derive the key from a secret, or to prevent an attacker from crafting a colliding key, or to guarantee that the key reveals nothing about the data. These are cryptographic requirements that belong to a separate layer (signatures, encryption, authentication).

Despite this, every content-addressable system pays the full cost of both roles because SHA-256 is the only universal identity generator available:

| Cost component | Value |
|---------------|-------|
| Gate equivalents | ~10,000 |
| Latency (hardware) | 64-75 cycles |
| Latency (software, ARMv8.4-A Firestorm) | 227 ns per op |
| Identifier size | 256 bits (32 bytes) |
| Collision handling | probabilistic, requires resolution table |
| Multi-axis query | requires separate index structures |

## The Alternative: Tagma Coordinate Composition

The Tagma coordinate space provides a closed-form deterministic mapping with three independent structural axes per coordinate. The full specification, composition formula, and compliance criteria are defined in the Tagma whitepaper [@tagma-wp]. The relevant property for identity generation is that each coordinate is simultaneously a unique identifier and a decomposable address, eliminating the need for separate index structures.

## The Identity Text

A coordinate is a value. Its text is a spelling of that value, and this section fixes both so that an address
means one thing in a file name, on the wire, and in a log line.

| Form | Definition | Size at depth 20 |
|---|---|---|
| value | N axis values, each below 11,172 | 2 bytes an axis |
| canonical text | N groups of three base-36 digits, lowercase, zero padded | 3 bytes an axis |
| Hangul rendering | N characters of the block, one per axis, each `U+AC00 + value` | 20 characters, 60 bytes in UTF-8 |

The text is normative in four properties.

| Property | Rule |
|---|---|
| alphabet | `0` to `9`, then `a` to `z`, in ascending code point order |
| width | three digits an axis, so the length is exactly 3N bytes and no axis shifts |
| case | lowercase only, and the uppercase form is refused on the way back |
| order | the text sorts as the value sorts, and a prefix of the text is a prefix of the axes |

The order property follows from the first two. A fixed width over an ascending alphabet makes a lexicographic
comparison the same comparison the value makes, which is what lets a key space be read as a coordinate space
with no separate index.

Two consequences are normative.

- The text is ASCII. It is a legal file name on every file system, and it needs no Unicode normalisation on
  either side of a conversion.
- The value is the authority. A structure inside a process holds the value, and the text exists where a
  surface needs it: a key, a file name, a wire field, a line of output.

### A worked example

Every axis value has a character of the block and a group of three digits.

| Form | Example | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| value | `3560` | inside a process |
| Hangul rendering | `맨` | a reader, a printed example |
| canonical text | `2qw` | a storage key, a file name, a wire field |

`2qw` is `2 x 1296 + 26 x 36 + 32`, which is `3560`, and `U+AC00 + 3560` is `맨`. The three name one axis
value, and the value is the authority over both spellings.

The whole space follows the same arithmetic at its two ends.

| Position | Value | Hangul | Canonical text |
|---|---:|---|---|
| first | 0 | `가` | `000` |
| last | 11,171 | `힣` | `8mb` |

At depth 20 an address is twenty of these groups. Its text is sixty bytes and its value is forty, and the
Hangul rendering is the same twenty values written as the block's own characters.

### Conversion

Two operations, and which one a caller gets is part of the specification.

| Operation | Input | Result | On bad input |
|---|---|---|---|
| parse | canonical text | the value | refused: a wrong length, a byte outside the alphabet, and an axis value at or above 11,172 are all `None` |
| render | the value | the canonical text | no bad input exists, because every value below 11,172 has exactly one text |

A refusal belongs to the boundary where the text entered, because that is the only place that can attribute it to a
writer. The operation that accepts any text is a label and is described below.

### Where each form lives

| Layer | Holds | Converts |
|---|---|---|
| the model and the arithmetic | the value | never |
| a container: a map, a set, an index, a filter | the value | at the edge that receives or emits text |
| a storage key and a physical file name | the text | once per surface crossing |
| the wire, a configuration file, a log line | the text | once per surface crossing |

The rule is one line long: a container holds the value and a boundary converts once. It holds as a property of the
types rather than as a convention of the callers, because a container keyed by the value cannot be written to with
text. A container keyed by the text is the failure this rule describes: it costs both conversions on every access
and it makes the text the thing the layer compares.

A record at the worked example's address is the file `facts/f_2qw.fact`, and a log line that names the same
record prints `2qw`, never the character. A depth-20 key has the same shape with sixty characters between the
prefix and the suffix. The container behind the process holds `3560`, so the lookup compares two bytes and
parses nothing.

### A label is a derived identifier

`from_label` hashes an arbitrary string into the coordinate space, and `resolve` answers with a label for any text
that is not canonical. Two consequences follow.

- A label names a record that was not addressed. It cannot be decomposed back into its input, so it is a name and
  not an address.
- A caller that must refuse a malformed address parses rather than resolves. The two operations differ in what they
  do with bad input, which is why they carry different names.

The choice of form inside a process follows from two measurements on the reference machine at depth 20.

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| axis composition | about 2 ns |
| value to canonical text | about 55 ns |
| canonical text to value | about 35 ns |

Composition is the operation this paper compares with SHA-256. The conversions are a boundary cost, paid once
per surface crossing. A public interface reaches the value through one parse, and everything behind it
compares values, which keeps the cost constant in the number of lookups rather than proportional to it.

The costs are also the evidence for the rule. A record layer that keyed its maps and its index by the text paid
both conversions on every lookup; keyed by the value it pays neither. Measured on the same machine at depth 20, an
intent lookup by fact fell from 33.4 to 13.0 microseconds per hundred calls, and a wanted-id scan over ten thousand
records from 133.6 to 95.6 microseconds. The medium's bytes did not move in either direction, because both
spellings of a depth-20 identity are sixty bytes.

## N-Coordinate Expansion

$$S(N) = 11,172^N \approx 10^{4.05N}$$

| Coordinates | Axes | Identifier space | Bytes | Equivalent to |
|-----------|------|-----------------|-------|---------------|
| 1 | 3 | 1.12 x 10^4 | 2 | Sensor tags |
| 2 | 6 | 1.25 x 10^8 | 4 | Database records |
| 3 | 9 | 1.39 x 10^12 | 6 | Distributed nodes |
| 6 | 18 | $1.94 \times 10^{24}$ | 12 | Below UUID ($3.4 \times 10^{38}$) |
| 10 | 30 | $3.03 \times 10^{40}$ | 20 | Exceeds UUID (128-bit) |
| 19 | 57 | $8.21 \times 10^{76}$ | 38 | Just below SHA-256 (256-bit) |
| 20 | 60 | $9.18 \times 10^{80}$ | 40 | Exceeds SHA-256 (256-bit) |

The coordinate space grows exponentially with coordinate count. Ten coordinates exceed the UUID (128-bit)
space; nineteen sit just below the SHA-256 space and twenty exceed it.

A two-coordinate address is two groups end to end. `2qw000` is the text of the values `3,560` and `0`, and
the block renders the same pair as `맨가`. Composition places the coordinates side by side without mixing them,
which is why an axis stays extractable at any depth.

Each CoordPath defines $3N$ independent axes whose semantics are entirely application-defined. The same N-coordinate sequence may encode geographic coordinates in one system and token sequence positions in another. The coordinate algebra -- composition, decomposition, linearisation, axis projection -- is invariant; the axis meaning is not. Tagma is an abstract coordinate algebra, not a fixed geometry.

{{< include ../../_include/bench/fig-bench-address-space.qmd >}}

## Index Elimination

| Layer | Current (SHA-256) | Tagma |
|------|-------------------|-------|
| Identity | SHA256(data) (256-bit opaque) | Tagma(i,m,f) = 0xAC00 + 588i + 28m + f (16-bit) |
| Index | separate: HashMap, BTree, OrderedIndex | none: identity = coordinate |
| Query | Vec ∩ Vec ∩ Vec -- O(K x N) intersection | decomposer() -- O(1) direct |

The arithmetic turns a partial query into a range rather than an intersection. Fixing the initial and the
medial leaves the final axis free, so `i = 6, m = 4` selects the twenty-eight consecutive values `3,640` to
`3,667`, which is the characters `머` to `멓`, which is the text `2t4` to `2tv`. A reader that holds the keys
answers the query by scanning that range, and a reader that holds a hash has no range to scan at all.

Two divisions recover a syllable's initial, medial, and final from its value, and an index recovers one
coordinate from a twenty-coordinate address. A hash supports neither operation, which is why a hash-keyed
store maintains the posting lists the next section compares against.

## Empirical Validation

A software proof of concept implements the Tagma coordinate in Rust, with 10 integration tests covering all 11,172 valid coordinates and all 54,364 invalid states.

| Metric | SHA-256 | Tagma (1-coord) | Tagma (6-coord) | Tagma (19-coord) |
|--------|---------|----------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Latency per op | 227 ns | 2 ns | 11 ns | 35 ns |
| Identifier size | 32 bytes | 2 bytes | 12 bytes | 38 bytes |
| Addressable space | $2^{256}$ | $1.12 \times 10^4$ | $1.94 \times 10^{24}$ | $2^{255.5}$ |
| Collision | probabilistic ($2^{-128}$) | deterministic zero | deterministic zero | deterministic zero |
| Multi-axis query | $O(K \times N)$ | $O(1)$ direct | $O(1)$ direct | $O(1)$ direct |

The figure for N coordinates is composition. The text conversions are a separate cost, given in The Identity Text.

{{< include ../../_include/bench/fig-bench-identity.qmd >}}

## Why Hangul

Why this block and not another? An identity primitive needs a code space with three properties at once: a
contiguous run, so an address is an offset from one base; a closed-form three-axis decomposition, so decoding
is arithmetic rather than a table; and BMP membership, so one identity is one 16-bit word. This block has all
three. It is 11,172 values, `19 x 21 x 28`, starting at U+AC00, with no irregular entries, and the whitepaper's
Script Comparison appendix finds no other block that does [@tagma-wp].

The writing system was designed in 1443 as a composition of initial, medial, and final, and the standard
encoded that composition directly: the three axes are the script's own, in the order the script composes them.
The requirement is met because the script was designed that way, not because an encoding was adapted to it.
The design predates the use by nearly six centuries.

The primitive takes the structure as the standard publishes it, and none of its constants is a computing
convention: the base, the radices, and the block are the standard's, fixed by a stability policy that no
implementation controls.

## Conclusion

An address is a coordinate, and a coordinate has one value with two spellings: the canonical text that a key, a
file name, and a wire field carry, and the block's own characters that a reader sees. The twenty values below
are the address the whitepaper gives its atom in the CoordSpace20 appendix [@tagma-wp]; this paper adds the
second spelling and the rule that produces it.

| Form | Address |
|---|---|
| Hangul rendering | `맨가억빈힣쐭롮직랯픟첹겨뇨됴듸뤼뮈븨싀쨔` |
| canonical text | `2qw00052t3m08mb4rx2ge5vl2b384f6gp04o1601mc1rs2m432g3l44hs5xw` |

| Axis | Value | Hangul | Canonical text |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 0 | 3,560 | `맨` | `2qw` |
| 1 | 0 | `가` | `000` |
| 2 | 6,581 | `억` | `52t` |
| 3 | 4,680 | `빈` | `3m0` |
| ... | | | |
| 19 | 7,700 | `쨔` | `5xw` |

Axes 4 through 18 follow the same rule: the value is the code point minus U+AC00, and the text is that value in
three base-36 digits. The value is the address and the text is that value in base 36; neither is a hash. What a
surface writes is a property of the surface; what the value is, is a property of the coordinate.
